History is not a river but a palimpsest, each era scrawling its testimony over the fading script of the last. We read the past through smudged glass, assembling fragments into narratives that comfort us with their illusory coherence.

The empire crumbles. It always crumbles. This is the one reliable grammar of civilization... the conjugation of rise and dissolution. Marble columns become road material. The forum becomes a field where goats graze among the ghosts of senators.

What survives is accidental. A letter preserved by volcanic ash. A song carried in the throat of a grandmother who never learned to write. The archive is ruthless in its omissions, cataloguing the declarations of kings while the lullabies of servants dissolve into air.

We study history to understand the present, or so we claim. But perhaps we study it for the same reason we press our tongues against a broken tooth... compulsively, painfully, drawn to the wound that shaped us. The past does not illuminate. It haunts. It lingers at the threshold, wearing familiar faces.
